title: What is Kundan jewellery and how is it made
description: Kundan is a stone-setting technique, not a stone. Learn how traditional and modern fashion Kundan jewellery is made, and how to judge a well-made piece.
intro: Kundan is a way of setting stones, not a type of stone. The word is generally understood to mean highly refined gold, and in the traditional method thin strips of that gold are pressed around each stone to hold it in place without claws or prongs. Most Kundan you see in shops today is the fashion version: glass stones set in a gold-plated brass frame, made to give the same royal look at a much friendlier price.

sections.heading: Where Kundan comes from
paragraphs: Kundan work is closely tied to the royal courts of North India, especially Rajasthan, and it flourished during the Mughal period. Jaipur and Bikaner are the cities most often named as its homes, and in many families the skill has been passed from one generation of karigars to the next.

That history is why Kundan still feels like 'shaadi jewellery' to most of us. It was made to be seen in candlelight and courtyards, so it is bold, flat-faced and full of reflected light rather than sharp sparkle.

sections.heading: How traditional Kundan is made, step by step
paragraphs: Real Kundan is slow work, usually split between several craftsmen who each handle one stage. The exact steps and their local names vary from workshop to workshop, but the broad sequence looks like this:
list: A gold frame is shaped by hand, with small hollow cups wherever a stone will sit.
Designs are engraved on the frame, and the back is often decorated with enamel (meenakari) in reds, greens and whites.
The hollow frame is filled with lac, a natural resin, which gives the piece body and a bed for the stones.
Each stone is placed in its cup and very pure gold foil is pushed in around its edges, layer by layer, until it is locked tight.
The piece is cleaned, polished and finished with silk thread or a dori for tying.

sections.heading: How fashion Kundan is made today
paragraphs: Fashion or imitation Kundan follows the same look with modern, affordable materials. The base is usually brass or another alloy, cast or pressed into shape with ready-made settings. The 'Kundan stones' are typically glass with a reflective foil backing, which is what gives them that flat, mirror-like glow.

Instead of hand-pushed gold foil, the stones are fixed with an adhesive or a lac-like compound, and the whole piece is gold plated, often in a warm or antique tone. Pearls, beads and meena-coloured drops are then added. Good fashion Kundan still needs skilled hands for setting and finishing; the difference is the metal and the stones, not the care.
This is the kind of piece most people buy for weddings and festivals today. Varaha's [Kundan necklace sets](/women/necklaces), for example, are brass with gold plating and Kundan stones.

sections.heading: Real Kundan or Kundan-look: which do you need?
paragraphs: Traditional gold Kundan is an heirloom purchase. It holds value because of the gold, but it is expensive, heavy and needs a trusted jeweller. Fashion Kundan gives you the same silhouette for a single function, a family wedding season, or simply to match many outfits without worrying about loss or theft.
A practical rule many families follow: buy one real piece if it matters to you, and build the rest of your festive wardrobe with good-quality fashion Kundan that you can actually wear freely.

sections.heading: How to judge a well-made Kundan piece
paragraphs: Whether you are buying online or at a shop, a few quick checks tell you a lot about the workmanship.
list: Stones should sit flush in their settings, with no tilt, gaps or glue marks around the edges.
The foil glow should look even across stones of the same colour, not patchy or dull in some.
The plating should be smooth on the back as well as the front, without bare spots near hooks.
Pearl strings and drops should be firmly attached, with no loose loops.
The dori or hook should be strong enough for the weight of the necklace.

sections.heading: Caring for Kundan so it keeps its shine
paragraphs: Water is Kundan's biggest enemy, because moisture can creep behind the stones and dull the foil. Put perfume and hairspray on before you wear the jewellery, wipe it with a soft dry cloth after use, and store it flat in a box or pouch with butter paper or tissue around it. Never soak a Kundan piece to clean it.

If a single stone does fall out, keep it safe in a small zip pouch rather than pushing it back with any glue you have at home. Some household glues can cloud the foil or the glass. A local jewellery repair shop can usually reset it neatly, and the piece will look as good as before.

faq.a: Traditional Kundan is made in gold. Most Kundan sold online today is fashion jewellery, usually brass or alloy with gold plating and glass stones.

faq.q: Is a Kundan stone a diamond?
faq.a: No. Kundan is a setting technique. In fashion pieces the stones are usually foil-backed glass. Uncut diamonds set this way are called Polki.
Avoid it. Water can seep behind the stones, dull the foil backing and loosen the setting. Wipe dry immediately if it gets splashed.

faq.q: Can I wear Kundan every day?
faq.a: Light Kundan earrings can be worn often, but heavy sets are best saved for occasions so the plating and stones last longer.
